report:
Conclusion: the claim is **broadly supported but qualified**. Across randomized placebo-controlled trials in chronic inflammatory diseases, anti-cytokine/immunomodulatory drugs show a **small-to-moderate reduction in depressive symptoms**, especially when depression is comorbid with inflammation; this is not proof they are stand-alone antidepressants. A systematic review/meta-analysis of chronic inflammatory-condition trials reported antidepressant activity for anti-cytokine treatment (https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/1522181/), and a larger mega-analysis concluded immunomodulatory drugs may help depressive symptoms comorbid with inflammatory disorders, with signals for some cytokine targets (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41380-019-0471-8).

However, certainty is limited: an earlier JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis found benefit but emphasized **high heterogeneity and risk of bias**, making mean effects uncertain (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/articlepdf/1916904/yoi140079.pdf). Effects also appear **biomarker-dependent**: in treatment-resistant depression, infliximab did not beat placebo overall, but helped patients with baseline hs-CRP >5 mg/L (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4015348/). So the fairest statement is: anti-cytokine drugs can reduce depressive symptoms in some people with chronic inflammatory conditions—likely those with elevated inflammation—but effects are modest, inconsistent across drugs/populations, and require monitoring for infection and other risks.
